# From Tehran to Tel Aviv: How press in Middle East is framing Iran war, ceasefire negotiations?

## Coverage across the Middle East reveals sharp divides over Iran’s nuclear program, the Hormuz crisis, President Trump’s diplomacy, and who bears responsibility for the widening confrontation.

[Follow us on **Google**](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=https://www.jpost.com/)

Smoke rises following an explosion, after Israel's Defence Minister Israel Katz said Israel had launched a pre-emptive attack against Iran, in Tehran, Iran February 28, 2026 in this screen grab taken from video.

(photo credit: WANA (WEST ASIA NEWS AGENCY) VIA REUTERS)

BySTEVEN GANOT/THE MEDIA LINE

As the [United States, Israel](https://www.jpost.com/international/article-898525), and [Iran](https://www.jpost.com/international/article-898509) move uneasily between escalation and diplomacy, news outlets across the Middle East are describing the crisis in sharply different terms.

For more stories from The Media Line go to[themedialine.org](https://themedialine.org/)

Gulf and Saudi-linked outlets are treating the war largely as a threat to energy security, shipping, and regional stability. Israeli media are warning that President Donald Trump may accept a weak deal that reopens the Strait of Hormuz while leaving Iran’s nuclear and missile programs largely intact.

# US energy secretary says lower gas prices will ultimately take resolution with Iran

## "The pathway to bring gasoline and diesel prices back down is to get more oil flowing through the Strait of Hormuz," US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in an interview.

[Follow us on **Google**](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=https://www.jpost.com/)

US Secretary of Energy Chris Wright speaks during a press conference discussing fertilizer policy at USDA Headquarters in Washington, DC, US, May 19, 2026.

(photo credit: REUTERS/Eric Lee)

ByREUTERS

US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Friday that lowering pump prices will ultimately take a resolution with Iran to get more oil flowing through the [Strait of Hormuz](https://www.jpost.com/middle-east/iran-news/article-897505).

Wright made the comments during an appearance at the Sable Offshore oil and gas facility near Santa Barbara, California, which restarted this year after [US President Donald Trump](https://www.jpost.com/middle-east/article-898463) invoked the Cold War-era Defense Production Act to supersede state laws.

Wright and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum used the media event to blame [California](https://www.jpost.com/middle-east/iran-news/article-897739)'s strict environmental policies for the state's sky-high gasoline prices, which hover around $6 a gallon.

# Putin says Russian troops are advancing on every front. In reality, the main battle is around Kramatorsk, and Ukraine could hold the city through 2026.

Source: Meduza

Russia’s military offensive accelerated in late May and early June after months of stagnation and Ukrainian counterattacks. Vladimir Putin has [declared](https://meduza.io/feature/2026/06/04/u-putina-sprosili-ne-pora-li-prekraschat-voynu-ved-reytingi-snizhayutsya-ekonomika-padaet-a-drony-byut-po-peterburgu-vot-chto-on-otvetil) that “there is no place without an offensive,” but the gains are limited to a few sectors. Ukraine’s defenses in Kostiantynivka — at the southern end of the greater Kramatorsk area — weakened sharply in recent weeks, allowing Russian forces to push toward the city center from two directions. Russia’s advance also continues east of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, along the southern bank of the Siverskyi Donets River and near the Siverskyi Donets-Donbas Canal. Russian pressure in the eastern Zaporizhzhia region has resumed in force after Ukrainian counterattacks halted the offensive there for several months. Elsewhere, Russia’s progress is stalling at best, and Moscow is unlikely to capture the greater Kramatorsk area and adjacent parts of the Donetsk region before the end of the year.

# India's Manufacturing Surge: A Path to Reduced Import Dependency

## India's manufacturing efforts show promise as import dependency decreases in key sectors like electricals and chemicals, despite global supply chain pressures. A Bank of Baroda report highlights sector-specific reductions in import dependence, attributing improvements to domestic manufacturing policies like Make in India and the India Semiconductor Mission 2.0.

![India's Manufacturing Surge: A Path to Reduced Import Dependency](https://devdiscourse.blob.core.windows.net/devnews/06_06_2026_16_12_04_8982177.jpg)

### Key Takeaways

India's strategic push towards enhancing its domestic manufacturing capabilities is showing encouraging signs, as a recent Bank of Baroda report reveals a decline in import dependency across several critical sectors. Areas such as electricals, chemicals, capital goods, and consumer durables are witnessing a shift towards self-reliance, even amidst ongoing global supply chain disruptions linked to the West Asia crisis.

The report highlights that while India's overall import-to-net-sales ratio has remained mostly stable over the years, there is a marked decrease in sector-specific import reliance. It analyzed 1,372 non-financial companies, noting a significant drop in the import-to-net-sales ratio,
